claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native, thin pre-formed oxide layer.
The native oxide layer on Q235 steel acts as a transient passive film.
A coherent thin oxide formed at room temperature can provide initial corrosion protection.
Annealing at 700–900 °C can transform the native oxide into either a stable protective scale or a porous, cracked structure.
The coherence or porosity of the thermally transformed oxide determines subsequent corrosion behavior during aggressive salt exposure.
Densification into a coherent, adherent oxide scale limits salt ingress and corrosion.
Thermal stresses can crack the oxide or produce a porous microstructure.
A cracked or porous oxide loses barrier protection and accelerates corrosion under aggressive salt exposure.

Q235 samples that develop a thermally stabilized, adherent oxide scale will exhibit minimal mass change and improved corrosion resistance relative to freshly prepared controls with minimal native oxide.
Samples whose oxide becomes porous or cracked will exhibit greater corrosion rates and mass change under otherwise identical aggressive conditions.
Freshly prepared Q235 surfaces with minimal native oxide are expected to corrode faster than specimens carrying a stabilized pre-exposure oxide.
The proposed mechanism applies when an ambient native oxide is followed by thermal cycling.
The proposed mechanism is not expected to apply when alloying, coatings, or contamination alter the surface chemistry.
The proposed mechanism is not expected to operate during purely inert high-temperature exposure in which oxidation reactions are suppressed.
A controlled study should compare room-temperature pre-oxidized and subsequently annealed Q235 specimens against freshly prepared Q235 controls under identical salt-exposure conditions.
Mass change, corrosion rate, oxide morphology, phase composition, adhesion, and continuity can be measured to test the proposed mechanism.
A lack of statistically significant corrosion-rate and scale-integrity differences, or a lack of correlation between oxide microstructure and corrosion performance, would falsify the hypothesis.
Previous relevant studies predominantly examined stainless, alloy, or boiler steels rather than Q235 steel.
